column4: The section's named cover (root غ ش ي), faces, and fire meet in this verse: fire envelops their faces.
The section links its opening al-Ghāshiya to later punishment; this verse names a غَاشِيَةٌ of God's punishment and the Hour's sudden arrival.
The section's boiling drink reverses life-giving rain: water like molten metal scalds faces (يَشْوِي الْوُجُوهَ) and is called a wretched drink.
As the section says, land revived after drying demonstrates resurrection; this verse says its reviver will surely revive the dead.
The section's camel is livestock whose skins make homes and whose fibers furnish them; the verse makes worldly shelter and furnishings from animal materials.
The section contrasts the drinkers' easy passage of milk (سَائِغًا لِلشَّارِبِينَ) with Hell's barely swallowed drink; this verse names milk easy for drinkers.
Against the section's drink that passes easily, this drink is barely swallowed (وَلَا يَكَادُ يُسِيغُهُ); thirst relief itself becomes torment.
The section explicitly joins the camel's food scene to the call “let the human look at his food” (فَلْيَنظُرِ الْإِنسَانُ إِلَىٰ طَعَامِهِ).
The section connects its word مُصَيْطِر (from س ط ر) with the record; here every small and great thing is مُسْتَطَر, written down.
This verse's own contribution is denial and turning away (كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ); preceding 75:31 says he neither believed nor prayed, the pairing the section invokes.
This verse says he neither believed nor prayed (فَلَا صَدَّقَ وَلَا صَلَّىٰ); 75:32 adds the denial and turning away named in the section.
The section's humbly lowered faces become forced abasement here: eyes are خَاشِعَة and humiliation overwhelms them when they are called to prostrate.
The section says eyes lower and voices grow quiet; here voices humble themselves (خَشَعَتِ الْأَصْوَاتُ) and only a whisper is heard on that Day.
The section's lowered gaze recurs as eyes humbled (خَاشِعَةٌ) on the Day, here following hearts that tremble.
On the promised Day eyes are humbled and humiliation covers them, matching the section's bowed faces under punishment.
Like the section's “you are only a reminder, not a controller,” this verse says the Messenger is no compeller and commands him to remind by the Quran.
This verse likewise says the Messenger is not a keeper over those who turn away; his charge is only conveyance, matching the section's limit on prophetic control.
The section contrasts toil with being satisfied by one's striving; this verse states that a person has only what he strives for (مَا سَعَىٰ).
The section's labor and satisfaction meet the claim that one's striving will be seen (سَوْفَ يُرَىٰ), before recompense.
The section's final account and the face satisfied with its effort meet the promise of full recompense (الْجَزَاءَ الْأَوْفَىٰ).
The section's toil, return, and account are staged as labor toward the Lord and a meeting with Him (كَادِحٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ ... فَمُلَاقِيهِ).
This verse gives the person whose record is handed rightward an easy account, making the section's final حساب a favorable reckoning for one outcome.
The section's account is illuminated by this verse's easy reckoning (حِسَابًا يَسِيرًا), one favorable outcome of the final reckoning.
The section says the Prophet does not keep the account; this verse gives each person an opened record on the Day of Resurrection.
The section names حِسَاب as its closing reckoning; here “enough for yourself today as accountant” (حَسِيبًا) joins the root's sufficiency and accounting senses.
The section's secondary sense of لَاغِيَة as something omitted from account has a Quranic counterpart: God does not hold people to account for لَغْو oaths.
Here too the oath's لَغْو is not charged, while deliberate oaths are; this makes the section's link between idle speech and what is left out of account concrete.
The section says no idle word is heard in the garden; this verse says its people hear neither لَغْو nor sin there.
The section's placed cups and unheard idle speech meet here: cups are passed around, with no لَغْو or sin in the garden.
This verse repeats the section's garden silence: they hear neither idle speech (لَغْوًا) nor falsehood there.
The section's garden has no idle speech; this verse says they hear no لَغْو there, except a greeting of peace.
The section's face-covering punishment has a dark counterpart: faces are covered as if with pieces of night, and their owners are people of the Fire.
The section's hot spring and fire meet the two disputing parties described here, one clothed in fire; the verse begins a punishment scene reversed by the garden.
This neighbor completes 22:19's fire scene: boiling water poured over heads melts what is in their bellies and their skins, matching the section's scalding-water imagery.
The section's non-nourishing thorn food has a counterpart in the tree of Zaqqum, whose fruit the damned eat and fill their bellies with.
After Zaqqum, this verse gives them boiling water to drink, joining the section's failed food and tormenting drink in one scene.
The section's flowing spring and drink are set against Hell's boiling water; this verse places pure garden rivers beside a drink of boiling water.
The section's hot fire and drink have a parallel punishment: the left-hand company is in scorching wind and boiling water (سَمُومٍ وَحَمِيمٍ).
This continues 56:42's punishment with a shade of black smoke, the inverse of the section's high garden and its comfortable furnishings.
The continuation says that shade is neither cool nor beneficial, reversing the section's running spring and garden comfort.
The section says rain's revival of earth proves resurrection; this verse sends water to a dead land, then says God will likewise bring out the dead.
This repeated sign says God sends water down and gives life to earth after its death, as in the section's explicit proof from revived soil.
The section's revived earth is described here: barren land stirs and swells when rain falls, producing growth before the verse turns to resurrection.
This completes 22:5's earth scene by stating that God gives life to the dead; the section likewise makes revived ground evidence for the Last Day.
After 22:5–6's revived soil and proof, this verse names the Hour and resurrection from graves, completing the section's inference from earth to the Day.
This verse asks who sends rain and revives earth after its death, answering “God”; the section uses the same revived-earth sign to make resurrection perceptible.
It directly joins looking at God's mercy, earth revived after death, and God's reviving the dead, matching the section's eye-to-earth-to-resurrection movement.
Winds and rain revive a dead land, “thus the resurrection”; this directly repeats the section's movement from soil's revival to human resurrection.
Measured rain revives a dead town, “thus you will be brought forth”; the verse makes the section's water-and-resurrection correspondence explicit.
Rain as provision revives earth after death; this verse groups that sign with winds and alternation of night and day, echoing the section's creation-based reminder.
The section joins the earth's revival to the garden; this verse sends blessed water that grows gardens and harvested grain.
The next verse names tall palm trees with clustered fruit, extending 50:9's rain-grown provision that echoes the section's food and garden.
This passage culminates in reviving a dead town and says “thus is the emergence,” the same soil-to-resurrection proof the section draws.
This concise formulation says God gives life to earth after its death, directly restating the section's soil-and-resurrection link.
The section's invitation to look at food continues into this verse: God pours water down, supplying the food whose origins the next lines reveal.
This continues 80:24's food inspection with the splitting of earth; the section also makes earth's surface part of what the eye must consider.
The section pairs raised couches with a raised sky; this verse says God built the heaven with might and is expanding it.
This verse says earth was spread (فَرَشْنَاهَا), giving the section's spread carpets and flattened ground a creation-level counterpart.
The section meets the raised couches and spread rugs with creation's raised heaven (رَفَعَهَا) and established balance.
The earth is laid out for creatures, echoing the section's flattened ground as the world's habitable floor beneath the garden's furnished room.
The sky's raised ceiling here parallels 88:18's raised heaven and the section's raised couches, linking the world's construction to the garden interior.
The earth is spread here after the sky is raised, the same vertical and horizontal construction the section connects to garden furnishings.
The spread earth yields its water and pasture; this completes the section's look from land and camel toward the provisions that sustain life.
Mountains are set here after earth and pasture, matching the section's sequence of looking at sky, mountains, and earth as formed things.
The verse calls earth a resting place, making the section's worldly ground a dwelling floor and its elevated garden couches a fitting reversal.
Mountains are made pegs here; their fixed height contributes the same formed landscape as the section's invitation to look at mountains.
This verse spreads earth, sets firm mountains, and grows measured things, paralleling the section's earth-and-mountain inspection as deliberate creation.
The verse commands people to look at the built and adorned sky, closely matching the section's repeated “look how it was made” appeal.
This continues the created-sky appeal with spread earth, firmly set mountains, and paired growth, matching the section's landscape sequence.
Earth is made a spread (بِسَاطًا) here; this wording directly meets the section's spread carpets and its earth flattened as a world-floor.
The spread earth lets people travel through broad paths, joining the section's walk from the opening arrival to the final return.
Earth is made a bed here and water produces varied plants; that dwelling-floor and provision meet the section's world tent, soil, and garden.
The section's two faces on that Day are elaborated as bright faces here, a specific reversal of the faces lowered in its opening scene.
The bright faces of 75:22 look toward their Lord, contrasting the section's humiliated, downward-looking faces with the garden's ease.
This verse gives the other side of 75:22–23: faces on that Day are gloomy, matching the section's punished faces.
Those gloomy faces expect a calamity here, completing the opposite face-scene to the section's radiant, satisfied garden faces.
The section distinguishes faces by their fate; this verse pictures faces on that Day radiant and rejoicing, the garden side of that contrast.
This completes 80:38's joyful faces and reinforces the section's contrast between the two groups' faces on the Day.
The opposing faces are dusty here, a dry-earth and humiliation image that recalls the section's lowered, punished faces.
Darkness covers those dusty faces, completing a face-covering scene opposite the section's soft, contented faces.
This begins the opposite outcome to the section's punished group: the people of the right are in a garden of ease.
The garden's lote trees are stripped of thorns, a precise reversal of the section's thorny darī as food that cannot nourish.
Extended shade here answers the section's blazing punishment with a garden scene of shelter and relief.
A flowing spring here directly answers the section's hot spring and matches its garden's running spring.
Abundant fruit in the garden reverses the section's meager, unsatisfying food.
The fruit is neither cut off nor forbidden, the inverse of the section's food that cannot satisfy hunger.
The garden's raised couches (فُرُشٍ مَّرْفُوعَةٍ) meet the section's elevated couches and its image of furnishing the garden room.
This garden has couches arranged in rows (سُرُرٍ مَّصْفُوفَةٍ), meeting the section's arranged pillows and spread furnishings.
Two garden springs flow here, a relief-bearing counterpart to the section's boiling spring and a parallel to its running garden spring.
Green cushions and fine carpets here furnish a garden scene, directly meeting the section's cushions, carpets, and furnished room.
The righteous drink a cup mixed with camphor here, a garden drink set against the section's difficult and scalding drink.
That cup comes from a spring made to flow; this joins the section's flowing garden spring and pleasant drink.
The garden's residents recline without sun or bitter cold, reversing the section's burning heat and matching its furnished repose.
Shade closes over the garden's residents and its fruits are brought near, developing the section's comfortable garden provision.
Silver vessels and cups are circulated here, a direct garden counterpart to the section's cups set out.
This verse specifies silver goblets measured to their measure, echoing the section's prepared cups and measured provision.
The garden's ginger-mixed drink is pleasant, adding a specific counterpart to the section's hot, barely swallowed drink.
The drink comes from a spring named Salsabil, expanding the section's garden image of a flowing spring and set cups.
A person receives his record in his right hand, meeting the section's final account and clarifying how one outcome is assessed.
The person knows he will meet his account, a direct articulation of the section's return followed by reckoning.
The right-hand recipient is in a pleasing life, a counterpart to the section's faces satisfied with their effort and garden ease.
“An elevated garden” (جَنَّةٍ عَالِيَةٍ) here exactly meets the section's high garden and gives the favorable account its setting.
They are told to eat and drink pleasantly for what they sent ahead, contrasting the section's unsatisfying food with reward for effort.
The other recipient is handed his record in his left hand, reversing 69:19 and making the section's two final outcomes concrete.
He is told to read his record, completing the account scene that the section leaves to God rather than the Messenger.
His wealth does not avail him (مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّي مَالِيَهْ), paralleling the section's repeated failure of worldly sufficiency.
His food is only ghislin, an explicit counterpart to the section's thorn food that neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger.
Only sinners eat that food, completing the punishment side of 69:36's failed nourishment and the section's divided outcomes.
The section says voluntary return makes one an أَوَّاب; this verse uses that label for Solomon, the servant who repeatedly turns back to God.
Job is called an أَوَّاب here, another direct Quranic use of the section's word for one who willingly returns.
This verse tells people to turn to their Lord before punishment arrives; it clarifies the section's contrast between voluntary return and the return that follows turning away.
The section's food-inspection word (source root ن ظ ر) meets this verse's waiting for a meal's readiness (نَاظِرِينَ إِنَاهُ); the shared root joins looking at food to its preparation.
This continues 52:23's garden cups and speech with servants circulating among them, adding the service surrounding the section's set-out vessels.
The verse asks whether people or heaven are harder to create, introducing 79:28's raised sky and the section's creation-based looking.
Bananas layered with fruit add to 56:28's thorn-free garden provision, a specific abundance opposite the section's hunger and darī.
This continues the elevated garden bedding with newly created companions, completing the garden's furnished comfort around the section's couches.
The easy-account recipient returns to his people rejoicing, matching the section's return and the garden face pleased with its outcome.
The other account recipient is given his record from behind his back, reversing the favorable reckoning of the section's garden group.
He calls for destruction after receiving that record, completing the section's contrast between contented and humiliated faces.
He enters blazing fire, completing 84:10–11's adverse account and echoing the section's hot punishment.
This continues 69:22's elevated garden with fruit clusters close at hand, adding garden provision to the section's high room and set food.
Zaqqum is introduced as food in the punishment scene, a specific parallel to the section's thorny, unsatisfying food.
This verse identifies Zaqqum as the sinner's food, directly extending the section's scene of food that cannot nourish.
The punishment's Zaqqum fruit is like molten metal boiling in bellies, intensifying the section's fiery food-and-drink image.
This completes the boiling image with a comparison to boiling water, parallel to the section's scalding drink.
The sinner is seized and dragged to the middle of the Fire, continuing the section's forced punishment scene.
Boiling water is poured over the sinner's head, a direct counterpart to the section's hot spring and fire.
This verse gives the left-hand group's food as Zaqqum, a parallel to the section's thorny food in Hell.
They fill their bellies with that tree's fruit, sharpening the contrast with the section's food that cannot satisfy hunger.
They drink boiling water after the tree's fruit, joining the section's unsatisfying food and scalding drink.
The drinkers gulp like thirsty camels, joining the section's singled-out camel with its contrast between easy milk and tormenting drink.
The verse calls this their welcome on the Day of Judgment, turning garden hospitality into punishment.
This verse answers 18:29's scalding drink with gardens, couches, silk, and ornaments, furnishing the garden counterpart developed in the section.
The couches are lined with brocade and their fruit is near, adding textile and provision details to the section's furnished garden room.
The garden's couches are richly woven, a direct furnishing parallel to the section's raised seats and arranged pillows.
The residents recline face to face on those couches, adding a specific posture to the section's furnished garden scene.
Gold platters and cups circulate in the garden, a specific parallel to the section's cups set out among its furnishings.
This verse commands looking at fruit as it forms and ripens, joining the section's gaze at created earth to food growing from it.
The heavens are raised without visible pillars, repeating the section's invitation to look at how the sky was raised.
The earth is spread with mountains, rivers, and varied growth, echoing the section's sequence of sky, mountain, and earth.
The verse joins unsupported heavens, mountains, animals, and rain-grown plants, extending the section's look from landscape to living provision.
Firm mountains and paths are set on earth here, a specific parallel to the section's mountains erected and earth spread.
Livestock are created for warmth and practical benefits, specifying the usefulness behind the section's invitation to look at the camel.
The herds are beautiful when brought back in the evening and sent out in the morning, echoing the section's day's walk and evening return around the camel image.
Livestock carry people and their burdens to distant lands, giving concrete travel use to the camel that opens the section's visual inquiry.
Livestock provide drink from their bellies and food, closely joining the section's camel scene to the milk passed easily to drinkers.
People are carried on livestock and ships, extending the section's camel from a created sign to a means of travel.
Created livestock are placed in human possession, paralleling the section's question about how the camel was created for use.
The livestock are made subject to people for riding and food, linking the section's camel and provisions.
Livestock yield benefits and drink, a direct parallel to the section's animal-derived furnishing and milk scenes.
The food inspection of 80:24 continues with grain grown from the split earth, identifying what that looking reveals.
This continuation names grapes and fodder, linking the earth's growth to food for people and animals.
Olives and date palms continue the food inventory that follows the section's call to inspect one's food.
Dense gardens extend the food-and-earth scene after 80:24's invitation to look at food.
Fruit and pasture continue the provision scene, joining the section's garden food to the camel's earthly nourishment.
The produce is provision for people and livestock, completing the food list that links the section's camel, earth, and eating.
Dead earth revived with grain for eating joins the section's soil-to-resurrection proof to its questions about food and creation.
Gardens of palms and vines with springs extend the same earth-revival sign into garden provision, matching the section's flowing spring and fruit.
The fruit is food from gardens people did not make, a specific reminder that the section's garden provisions are created and provided.
This verse says no small or great deed is omitted from the opened record, repeating the section's link between its account and what is written.
Two recorders sit on the right and left, giving a concrete account-keeping scene behind the section's claim that the Messenger is not the keeper.
No word is spoken without a watcher ready to record it, joining the section's silence about idle speech to its reckoning and record.
Every atom's weight of good will be seen, specifying the small-scale measure behind the section's work and final account.
Every atom's weight of evil will likewise be seen, completing the section's account of both outcomes.
Scales of justice are set on the Day and no soul is wronged even by a mustard seed, making the section's account a precise measure.
The section names the ح س ب root in its sufficiency sense; this verse says “Allah is sufficient for us,” alongside reliance on Him.
The same root's sufficiency sense appears in “Allah is sufficient for you,” distinct from its accounting use in the section's final verse.
The Messenger says “Allah is sufficient for me,” a further Quranic use of the section's named root in its sufficiency sense.
Every soul is returned to God and confronted with what it did, directly joining the section's return to its accounting.
People return to God and are told what they did, echoing the section's pairing of return with account.
All return to their Lord, who informs them of their deeds, matching the section's sequence of return and reckoning.
The peaceful soul offers another face of the section's satisfied outcome before its return to God and entry into the garden.
The soul is told to return to its Lord pleased and pleasing, a direct parallel to the section's satisfied face and final return.
The returning soul is welcomed among God's servants, completing 89:28's return as a communal garden entry beside the section's garden gathering.
The returned soul is told to enter Paradise, completing the section's link between return and the high garden.
The section's mountain image meets its secondary return root here: mountains are commanded to join David in praise, using the A-W-B root.
This verse calls the repentant “awwābīn”; it is another use of the section's word for a person who turns back to God.
Faces on that Day are divided between brightness and darkness, repeating the section's paired faces and their opposed outcomes.
The bright-faced group is in God's mercy, specifying the garden side of the section's two faces on that Day.
Those who do good receive more and have no dust or humiliation on their faces, a specific reversal of the section's punished faces.
Mountains are moved away on the Hour, reversing the section's view of them firmly set in the created landscape.
A pregnant she-camel is abandoned when the Hour arrives; this is a specific inversion of the section's useful, observed camel, though the link is distant.
Earth and mountains are lifted and crushed on the Day, reversing the section's spread earth and erected mountains.
The sky splits on that Day, a specific reversal of the section's raised and constructed heaven.
Mountains are moved and earth exposed on the gathering Day, undoing the formed landscape the section asks the eye to inspect.
The question about what happens to mountains on the Day returns to the section's question of how they were set up.
The mountains are crushed to dust, a direct reversal of their firm erection in the section's creation scene.
The land is left level, with no crookedness or unevenness, reversing the section's spread earth as a prepared surface.
